name: Damascus
info: Damascus is the capital of Syria, on a plateau watered by the Barada River below the Anti-Lebanon mountains. First settled in the 3rd millennium BCE, it was an Aramaean capital, a Roman city and the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate.

facts.founded: First settled in the 3rd millennium BCE; carbon-14 dating at Tell Ramad on its outskirts suggests occupation from about 6300 BCE, but no large-scale settlement lay within the present walls until the second millennium BCE. Greek myths and Josephus name founders of their own.
facts.where: On a plateau 680 metres above sea level, about 80 km inland from the Mediterranean, in south-western Syria, on the eastern foothills of the Anti-Lebanon mountains and the Barada River.
facts.known: Aram-Damascus; the Roman plan of the Old City; capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750; the Umayyad Mosque; the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods; the sack by Timur in 1401; the Ottoman Hajj caravans; capital of the French Mandate and of independent Syria
facts.today: Damascus is the capital and largest city of Syria, and its Old City is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Damascus became prominent as the capital of the Aramaean state of Aram-Damascus, passed through Assyrian, Hellenistic and Roman hands, and was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750.
After the Abbasids moved the seat of power to Baghdad it declined, then regained importance under the Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans, and was sacked by Timur in 1401.
It became the capital of the French Mandate for Syria in 1920 and has remained the capital of independent Syria, which became fully independent in 1946.
dyk: The English word damask comes from the patterned Byzantine and Chinese silks that reached the West through Damascus, one of the western termini of the Silk Road.
ev: Ezron captures Damascus and founds the independent state of Aram-Damascus
Pompey annexes western Syria and the Romans take Damascus
Khalid ibn al-Walid conquers Damascus for the Rashidun Caliphate
Mu'awiya makes Damascus the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate
The Abbasids take the city and the seat of Islamic power moves to Baghdad
Timur sacks Damascus and burns the Umayyad Mosque
The Ottomans take Damascus from the Mamluks
A French army enters Damascus, which becomes the capital of the Mandate for Syria

sections.origins:
Damascus lies on a plateau 680 metres above sea level, about 80 km inland from the Mediterranean, sheltered by the Anti-Lebanon mountains and supplied with water by the Barada River. It stood at a crossing of the north-south route linking Egypt with Asia Minor and the east-west desert route linking Lebanon with the Euphrates valley. The river rises from mountain streams fed by melting snow, and the city is surrounded by the Ghouta, irrigated farmland where vegetables, cereals and fruit have been grown since ancient times.

The city is held to have been first settled in the 3rd millennium BCE. Carbon-14 dating at Tell Ramad, on its outskirts, suggests that the site may have been occupied from the second half of the seventh millennium BCE, possibly around 6300 BCE, and settlement in the wider Barada basin dates to 9000 BCE, but no large-scale settlement lay within Damascus's present walls until the second millennium BCE. Its name appears in the geographical list of Thutmose III in the 15th century BCE and in the Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE, where Dimasqu is ruled by Biryawaza. In Genesis it exists at the time of the War of the Kings, and Josephus gave Uz, son of Aram, as its founder. Greek myths gave other founders and explanations of the name Damaskós.
sections.growth:
Damascus became an important city with the arrival of the Aramaeans in the 11th century BCE. They built a water system of canals and tunnels that made the most of the Barada, which the Romans and Umayyads later improved and which still forms the basis of the water supply of the old part of the city. Under the Romans the city prospered during the Pax Romana. Trade routes from southern Arabia, Palmyra, Petra and the Silk Road converged on it, and it supplied the Roman demand for eastern luxuries. It became a metropolis by the beginning of the 2nd century, and in about 125 Hadrian promoted it to Metropolis of Coele-Syria.

Under the Umayyads the city was the capital of an empire stretching from the Iberian Peninsula to the Indus. From 685 Abd al-Malik introduced a distinctive Islamic coinage and Arabic replaced Greek as the language of administration. The Grand Mosque was begun in 706 and finished by 715, and the city grew beyond its old walls to the slopes of Mount Qasioun. The Ayyubid period brought another phase of expansion, with new madrasas, mosques and hospitals inside and outside the walls, and the district of al-Salihiyah grew on the slopes of the mountain. In the Ottoman period Damascus was the departure point of one of the two great Hajj caravans to Mecca, though Aleppo was more populous and commercially more important for most of those centuries.
sections.rulers:
Damascus was the capital of Aram-Damascus from 965 BCE. The Assyrians subdued it in the 8th century BCE, a revolt of 727 BCE was put down, and it later passed into the orbit of Egypt under Necho II and to Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon by 572 BCE. Alexander the Great conquered it, and after his death in 323 BCE it passed repeatedly between the Seleucid and Ptolemaic empires. Pompey annexed western Syria in 64 BCE, and the city became part of the Decapolis and the Roman province of Syria. The Sasanian general Shahrbaraz captured it in 613, and it was in Sasanian hands until near the end of the war of 602 to 628.

Khalid ibn al-Walid took it for the Rashidun Caliphate in 634, and after the Muslim victory on the Yarmouk in 636 Mu'awiya governed it from 639. He made it the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate in 661, until Marwan II moved the capital to Harran in 744. The Abbasids conquered the city on 25 August 750, and it was then held by the Tulunids, Qarmatians, Ikhshidids and Fatimids. The Seljuqs ruled from 1079, followed by the Burids, Nur ad-Din from 1154 and Saladin's Ayyubid line. The Mamluks took it in 1260 and the Ottomans in 1516. The Ottomans stayed for about 400 years, apart from Ibrahim Pasha of Egypt's occupation from 1832 to 1840.
sections.life:
The Old City keeps the rectangular shape of the Roman city, about 1,500 by 750 metres inside a wall with seven gates, of which only the eastern gate, Bab Sharqi, kept its Roman form. Its two main axes were the Decumanus Maximus, now the Via Recta or Straight Street, and the Cardo. Roman Damascus lies mostly up to five metres below the modern city. The old borough of Bab Tuma grew at the end of the Roman and Byzantine era around the local Eastern Orthodox community, and according to the Acts of the Apostles Saint Paul and Saint Thomas both lived there. When Muslim armies took the city the population remained mostly Christian, with a growing Muslim community.

The Seljuqs reversed Shia gains in the city and expanded religious life through private endowments that paid for madrasas and hospitals, and Damascus became an important centre of Islamic thought. Under the Ayyubids the Al-Murshidiyya, Al-Jaharkasiyya, Al-Sahiba, Al-Shibliyya, Al-Rukniyya and Al-Shamiyya madrasas were founded. Under the Ottomans Christians and Jews were dhimmis, allowed to practise their religions under restrictions. An Ottoman census recorded 10,423 households in the early 16th century, and a missionary put the population at about 140,000 in 1867, of whom 30,000 were Christians and 10,000 Jews. Mimar Sinan designed the Sulaymaniyya Takiyya for pilgrims on the road to Mecca, completed in 1559.
sections.crises:
Damascus suffered many sieges and disasters. The Assyrians plundered the kingdom outside its walls in the 9th century BCE. After the Abbasid conquest in 750 the Umayyad family cemetery was desecrated and the city walls were torn down. On 24 November 847 a multiple earthquake struck and destroyed Damascus, killing about 70,000 people. In 998 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim executed hundreds of its citizens for incitement. In 1129 about 6,000 Isma'ili Muslims were killed in the city after rumours of a plot, and in 1148 a crusader siege failed.

The Mongols entered on 1 March 1260 and Ghazan besieged the city in 1299 to 1300. The Black Death of 1348 to 1349 killed as much as half of the population. Timur besieged Damascus in 1400 and sacked it on 17 March 1401. The Umayyad Mosque was burnt, men and women were enslaved and many of the artisans were taken to Samarkand. Many other people were slaughtered, and their heads were piled outside the north-east corner of the walls, at a place still called Burj al-Ru'us, the tower of heads. In June 1860 several thousand Christians were killed when fighting between Druze and Maronites spilled over from Mount Lebanon, and the Christian quarter was burnt. The Algerian exile Abd al-Qadir and his soldiers sheltered many others. In 1926 French bombing and shelling during the Great Syrian Revolt burned the area between Al-Hamidiyah and Medhat Pasha souqs, known since as al-Hariqa, the fire. Reporter George Seldes counted 308 bodies and suggested that the maximum might be one thousand.
sections.legacy:
The Umayyad Mosque, begun in 706 on the site of a Byzantine church dedicated to John the Baptist, a Hellenistic temple of Zeus and a Roman temple of Jupiter, is one of the oldest sites of continuous prayer since the rise of Islam. A shrine inside is said to contain the body of Saint John the Baptist, and Saladin's mausoleum stands in the gardens outside. The Roman layout of the Old City, the Straight Street named in Acts 9:11, the Citadel and the Ottoman and Ayyubid madrasas and mosques also survive. The Old City was listed as a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1979.

The city's name lives on in the English word damask. In the 20th century nationalist feeling grew against Ottoman rule, and Jamal Pasha hanged a number of patriotic intellectuals in 1915 and 1916. The Arab Revolt and British forces approached Damascus in 1918, and Faisal ibn Hussein was proclaimed king of Syria. A French army defeated a small Syrian force at Maysalun in 1920 and made Damascus the capital of the Mandate for Syria. The French agreed to leave in 1946. In the Syrian civil war fighting reached the outskirts of the city in 2012, the Ghouta suburb was bombed in 2017 and 2018, and rebels entered Damascus on 8 December 2024. The 2004 census gave the city 1,552,161 people, and it is the centre of a metropolitan area estimated at 5 million.

summary: Damascus, on the Barada below the Anti-Lebanon mountains, was the capital of Aram-Damascus, a Roman city and the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. It was sacked by Timur in 1401 and became the capital of Syria. Its Old City is a World Heritage Site.
notes: START: the article says 'first settled in the 3rd millennium BCE' (lead) but the History says Tell Ramad may date to c. 6300 BCE and wider Barada basin settlement to 9000 BCE, with no large-scale settlement within the walls until the second millennium BCE. I used -2500 circa true and gave both in facts.founded and origins.
No 'History of Damascus' article was supplied; only the city's own article was used.

The article says Ezron founded Aram-Damascus in 965 BCE; it also says the Aramaeans entered the city 'without battle' in the 11th century BCE. Both kept. Hazael is said to have killed Hadadezer; I left this out.
Hellenistic: the article says Demetrius III 'rebuilt the city' as Demetrias; left out as undated. Aretas IV/Nabatean control left out as unproven per the article.
The article's population of Aleppo vs Damascus and the 'fourth-holiest city in Islam' claim ('according to some') left out. 'Oldest capital city in the world' left out.
Ottoman census: the article gives 10,423 households without a year beyond the early 16th century context; I wrote 'early 16th century' as the paragraph places it after the 1516 conquest (a hedge).

Modern period: civil war told as bare dated facts; the article's liveability rankings, the 2025 Israeli strikes and Netanyahu demands, and reconstruction projects left out. Population: 2004 census figure given with its year; the metropolitan estimate of 5 million has no year in the article.

The Abbasid 'treasury dome' of 789, the Tulunid shrine to Mu'awiya, the Burid details and the Mongol 1300 episode were left out for length. Hajj caravan statement is as the article gives it. 'Seldes ... maximum might be one thousand' is attributed to him as the article does.
The 1926 bombing: the article quotes General Sarrail giving the civilian population time to evacuate; left out. Event labelled 1920 for the French entry (article date).
